front.title: The agent URI Scheme and Verifiable Agent Identity

abstract.t: Software agents increasingly act on the Internet on behalf of people and organizations: they call APIs, browse websites, and delegate work to other agents. Protocols such as A2A and MCP define how agents communicate, but there is no interoperable way to answer a prior question: which agent is this, and how can its claims be verified?

This document defines the agent URI scheme as a stable, human-readable identifier for an agent, a deterministic mapping from that identifier to an HTTPS-hosted Agent Identity Document, anchoring of the agent's keys to a web origin or a Decentralized Identifier, and signed statements that bind the agent to its protocol metadata. It also defines profiles that let an agent prove its identity on HTTP requests, building on HTTP Message Signatures for automated traffic, and that let short-lived agent instances act under the agent's identity using the WIMSE Workload Identity Token format. It deliberately does not define how agents communicate, describe their capabilities, or are invoked.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Agents are now first-class actors on the Internet. A single user task can cause an agent to call dozens of APIs and other agents, each of which needs to decide whether to serve the request. Today those services can see a TLS client, an IP address, perhaps an OAuth access token issued to some client, and a User-Agent string that anyone can forge. They cannot reliably tell which agent is calling, or whether the protocol metadata it advertises was really published by whoever controls it.

Communication protocols already exist. defines agent-to-agent interaction and an Agent Card; defines how agents reach tools and publishes server metadata; OpenAPI describes HTTP APIs. Each of these describes how to talk to an endpoint. None of them defines a portable answer to who an agent is that works across all of them.
This document defines that missing identity layer. Its core ( to ) is:

li.t: A name. The agent URI (e.g., agent://example.com/planner) is a stable, human-readable identifier for an agent ().
A document. Every agent URI maps deterministically to an HTTPS URL that serves an Agent Identity Document listing the agent's claimed operator, public keys, and links to its protocol metadata ().
An anchor. The agent's keys are trusted because of where the document is served (the origin derived from the agent URI) or because of a Decentralized Identifier bound to the agent URI ().
Statements. The agent signs statements binding itself to specific protocol metadata, so that metadata can be hosted, mirrored, or indexed anywhere ().

section.t: On top of the core, this document defines profiles that are deliberately separable and are expected to track related IETF work:

li.t: a request-signing profile of ();
an agent-instance profile that reuses the WIMSE Workload Identity Token format with AID-based trust (); and
OAuth 2.0 bindings ().
Identify, do not invoke. An agent URI names an agent. It is not a locator for an endpoint and carries no invocation parameters.

Reuse before invent. Every mechanism is a profile of an existing or in-progress standard: HTTPS and well-known URIs , JWK , JWS , HTTP Message Signatures as profiled by , the WIMSE Workload Identity Token format , OAuth 2.0, and DIDs .
Anchor trust outside the document being verified. A key is trusted because of the origin or DID it is published under, never because a document names it about itself.

Separate the name from the long-lived identity when needed. Domains change hands; agents get renamed and sold. The scheme supports a stable cryptographic identifier behind the human-readable name, with continuity for verifiers that have seen it before ().
Authenticate keys, not claims. Verification establishes control of keys anchored to an agent URI. Everything else an agent says about itself, including who operates it, remains a claim.
Work for agents that live for seconds. Most agent executions are ephemeral. Instances act under the identity of their agent without being individually published.

section.name: Non-Goals
section.t: The following are explicitly out of scope:

li.t: Communication semantics, message formats, task lifecycles, and invocation. These belong to A2A, MCP, OpenAPI-described APIs, and similar protocols.
Capability, skill, or tool description. Protocol metadata documents (for example, an A2A Agent Card or an MCP server card) remain authoritative for these.
Transport bindings.
Verification of organizations. This document does not verify that the operator an agent claims is real or actually operates it.
Search, ranking, or registry services. This document makes identity verifiable so that any registry can index agents without being trusted.
Reputation, pricing, payments, and service levels.
Authorization policy. Knowing who an agent is does not grant it anything.

section.name: Conventions and Terminology
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.
This document uses the terms "JSON object", "member", and "string" from , and "Dictionary", "Item", and "String" from .

dd.t: A software system that acts autonomously or semi-autonomously, typically on behalf of a person or organization.
The person or organization that an agent claims is accountable for it.
An agent URI as defined in . The human-readable name of an agent.
A JSON document, retrieved by dereferencing an agent URI, that lists the agent's claimed operator, keys, and links ().
The HTTPS URL that an agent URI maps to (), either under /.well-known/agent on the agent URI's host or at a location delegated through DNS ().
The tuple ("https", host, 443) for the host of the AID URL. AID URLs never contain a port.
A public key anchored to an agent ().
The JWK SHA-256 Thumbprint of an Agent Key ().
A running, typically short-lived execution of an agent that holds its own key pair and acts under the agent's identity ().
Any party that checks an agent's identity: a website or API receiving requests, an authorization server, a registry, or another agent.

section.name: Overview

figure.name: From agent URI to verifiable identity
figure.artwork: agent://example.com/planner (name) | | deterministic mapping v https://example.com/.well-known/agent/planner (AID URL) | +--------------------+---------------------+ | | | operator (claim) keys (JWK Set) links (rel, href) | | origin-anchored: trusted via HTTPS A2A Agent Card, DID-anchored: keys from DID document MCP server card, OAuth client metadata

section.t: A typical verification, for a request received by an API:

li.t: The request carries an HTTP message signature and a Signature-Agent member whose value is the AID URL of agent://example.com/planner.
The verifier derives the agent URI from the AID URL and retrieves the AID (or uses a cached copy).
The verifier finds the anchored key identified by the signature and verifies the signature and the request content.

The verifier now knows that the request was made by a holder of a key anchored to agent://example.com/planner. It also has the operator the agent claims, which it must not treat as verified (). Whether to serve the request remains a policy decision.

section.name: Syntax
section.t: The following ABNF uses fragment from and ALPHA and DIGIT from .

figure.name: ABNF for the agent URI
figure.sourcecode:
agent-uri = "agent://" agent-host [ name-path ] [ "#" fragment ]
agent-host = dns-name dns-name = label 1*( "." label ) label = let-dig [ *61( let-dig / "-" ) let-dig ] let-dig = ALPHA / DIGIT
name-path = 1*8( "/" name-segment ) name-segment = lc-let-dig [ *61( lc-let-dig / "-" ) lc-let-dig ] lc-let-dig = %x61-7A / DIGIT ; a-z, 0-9

section.t: Additional constraints:

li.t: dns-name MUST contain at least two labels (as required by the ABNF), MUST NOT exceed 253 octets, and its final label MUST contain at least one ALPHA character. This excludes IPv4 addresses in dotted-decimal form and single-label names such as localhost.
Internationalized domain names MUST be represented as A-labels . IP literals and userinfo are not permitted.
An agent URI MUST NOT contain a port, so that an agent's identity depends only on its host and name.
An agent URI MUST NOT contain a query component.
An agent URI with an empty name-path (e.g., agent://planner.example.com) identifies the domain's root agent.

section.t: Examples:

li.t: agent://example.com/planner#kPrK_qmxVWaYVA9wwBF6Iuo3vVzz7TxHCTwXBygrS4k (a reference to one of the agent's keys; see )

section.name: Normalization and Comparison
section.t: The canonical form of an agent URI is produced by:

li.t: Lowercasing the scheme and dns-name.
Converting any U-labels to A-labels.
Removing a ":443" port, or a ":" followed by an empty port, after the host. Any other port is a deviation that MUST be rejected.
Removing a single trailing "/" if present.

section.t: Parsers MAY accept input that differs from the ABNF only by the deviations corrected above, and MUST normalize it. Any other deviation (uppercase in name-path, percent-encoding, dot-segments, a query, a trailing "." on the host) MUST be rejected.

Two agent URIs identify the same agent if and only if their canonical forms, with any fragment removed, are identical octet strings. In particular, agent://example.com/planner and agent://planner.example.com are different agents, even if the same operator runs both.
Agent URIs in AIDs, statements, credentials, and tokens MUST be in canonical form and MUST NOT contain a fragment, unless a fragment is explicitly permitted.

section.name: Dereferencing
section.t: An agent URI is dereferenced by mapping it to its AID URL. Unless the host delegates its AID URLs through DNS (), the AID URL is:
For example:

table.name: Agent URI to AID URL mapping

section.t: The root agent uses the reserved segment _, which cannot appear in a name-segment. This allows the root AID and named AIDs to coexist on static file hosting.

This mapping is purely syntactic and is reversible: an HTTPS URL is a well-known AID URL if and only if it has no query or fragment and applying the reverse mapping yields an agent URI that is valid and canonical. No registry or index needs to be fetched to dereference an agent URI.

section.name: DNS Delegation
section.t: An operator that cannot serve /.well-known/agent from an agent URI's host, for example because the domain has no web server, can delegate that host's AID URLs to another HTTPS location. It does so by publishing a TXT record at the owner name _agent.<dns-name> (), in a zone signed with DNSSEC :

When a TXT record consists of several character-strings, they are concatenated without separators before processing. A delegation record is a TXT record whose value begins with v=agent1 followed by the end of the value, whitespace, or ;. Its value has the following syntax, where WSP is from :

figure.name: ABNF for a delegation record
figure.sourcecode: delegation = "v=agent1" *( *WSP ";" *WSP [ param ] ) param = pname "=" pvalue pname = 1*( ALPHA / DIGIT / "-" ) pvalue = 1*( %x21-3A / %x3C-7E ) ; visible characters except ";"

section.t: The base parameter is REQUIRED and MUST appear only once. Its value MUST be an HTTPS URL consisting of https://, a lowercase host that meets the constraints on dns-name in , and an optional path. The path MUST NOT end with "/" and MUST NOT contain percent-encoded octets, empty segments, or dot-segments; the URL MUST NOT contain userinfo, a port, a query, or a fragment. Other parameters MUST be ignored.
When delegation applies to a host, the AID URLs of its agent URIs are:
For example, with the record in , agent://example.com/planner maps to https://agents.example.net/example-com/planner.

A verifier that supports delegation MUST either perform DNSSEC validation itself or rely on a validating resolver that it trusts and reaches over a channel that protects integrity, such as a resolver on the same host or one reached using DNS over TLS . A validation result reported by an untrusted resolver, or over an unprotected network path, MUST NOT be used. It processes the agent URI's host as follows:

li.t: It queries TXT records for _agent.<dns-name>.
If DNSSEC validation establishes the response as insecure, it ignores any delegation record and uses the well-known mapping. If the response is bogus or indeterminate, dereferencing fails.
If the response is secure and contains no delegation record (including a secure denial of existence), it uses the well-known mapping.
If the response is secure and contains exactly one delegation record that is valid, delegation applies, and the verifier MUST NOT use the well-known mapping for that host.
If the response is secure and contains more than one delegation record, or one that is not valid, dereferencing fails. The verifier MUST NOT fall back to the well-known mapping.

section.t: Delegation applies only to agent URIs whose dns-name is exactly the owner name without its _agent label; subdomains are not covered. Verifiers SHOULD cache delegation results for the TTL of the response, including negative results for the negative-caching TTL.

Operators that delegate MUST NOT also publish AIDs under /.well-known/agent on the delegating host (). Support for delegation is OPTIONAL for verifiers. A verifier that does not support it uses the well-known mapping for every host, and so cannot verify delegated agents; operators that need every verifier to recognize their agents SHOULD use the well-known mapping instead.
The AID Origin of a delegated agent is the origin of its delegated AID URL. Apart from how the AID URL is formed, retrieval and validation are unchanged ().

section.name: Fragments
section.t: A fragment in an agent URI identifies an Agent Key by its Key Identifier (). No other fragment semantics are defined.

section.name: Format
section.t: An AID is a JSON object served with media type application/agent-id+json (). It has the following members:

dd.t: REQUIRED. String. The canonical agent URI that this document describes.
REQUIRED. Object stating who the agent claims is accountable for it, with members name (REQUIRED, string) and url (OPTIONAL, string, HTTPS URL). These values are self-asserted ().
REQUIRED for origin-anchored agents; MUST be absent for DID-anchored agents. A JWK Set containing the agent's public keys ().
OPTIONAL. String. A DID whose DID document is the anchor for this agent's keys ().
OPTIONAL. String. A display name for people. It has no identity semantics.
OPTIONAL. String. The time the document was last changed, as an RFC 3339 timestamp.

section.t: Members not defined here MUST be ignored by verifiers that do not understand them. Extension member names SHOULD be namespaced (e.g., "acme_tier") to avoid collision with future versions of this document.
An AID MUST NOT exceed 64 KiB.

section.name: Key Identifiers
section.t: Every Agent Key is identified by its Key Identifier: the base64url-encoded JWK SHA-256 Thumbprint of the key, computed as specified in for EC keys and in for OKP keys. This is the same identifier uses for keyid.

Key Identifiers are used everywhere a key is named in this document: in the kid of JWKs in an AID, in agent URI fragments, in the JWS kid header of statements and Workload Identity Tokens, and in the keyid signature parameter of request signatures.

Verifiers MUST compute the thumbprint of each candidate key themselves and select keys by comparing it with the presented Key Identifier. They MUST NOT rely on an operator-supplied kid or DID verification method id to select a key.
For DID-anchored agents, each verification method is converted to a JWK before the thumbprint is computed:

li.t: a publicKeyJwk value is used as-is (private members MUST NOT be present);
a publicKeyMultibase value that is a Multikey encoding of an Ed25519 public key (base58btc with the 0xed01 header, as defined in ) is converted to an OKP JWK with "crv": "Ed25519"; and
verification methods in any other representation MAY be supported; those a verifier cannot convert are ignored.

section.name: Key Purposes
section.t: Agent Keys are used for two purposes:

dd.t: Signing Agent Statements () and Workload Identity Tokens for instances ().
Signing HTTP requests directly as the agent ().

section.t: For DID-anchored agents, a key is usable for assertion only if it is referenced from the DID document's assertionMethod relationship, and for authentication only if it is referenced from authentication . Verifiers MUST enforce these relationships.

For origin-anchored agents, a JWK in keys MAY carry an agent_use member (): an array containing one or both of the strings "assertion" and "authentication". A key is usable only for the purposes listed; a key without agent_use is usable for both. Verifiers MUST enforce agent_use. A key whose agent_use is not an array of strings (for example, a bare string), or contains no recognized value, MUST be ignored; it is never treated as unrestricted. An AID in which two JWKs have the same Key Identifier MUST be rejected, so that purposes cannot be combined across entries for the same key material. Operators SHOULD give every key a single purpose, so that a key held by a running agent for request signing cannot mint Workload Identity Tokens or sign statements ().

section.name: Links
section.t: Each link object has the following members, with the semantics of Web Linking :

dd.t: REQUIRED. String. A registered link relation type or a URI.
REQUIRED. String. An absolute HTTPS URL.
OPTIONAL. String. The media type of the target.
OPTIONAL. String. An Agent Statement () about the target.

section.t: Link relations expected to be common include:

tr.td: An OpenAPI or other API description
The agent's OAuth Client ID Metadata Document ()
A JWK Set referred to by other metadata, such as a jwks_uri ()

section.t: A link whose href has the same origin as the AID Origin is trusted to the same degree as the AID itself. To compare, the verifier lowercases the href host, converts it to A-labels, and uses port 443 if none is present; the result must equal the AID Origin exactly (). No other normalization is applied; in particular, a trailing "." is not removed from the host. A link to any other origin MUST carry a statement, and verifiers MUST ignore cross-origin links without a valid statement (). Because verifier-initiated fetches never follow redirects (), a same-origin href cannot acquire the same-origin exemption for content served from another origin.

For DID-anchored agents the same-origin exemption does not apply: every link MUST carry a statement signed with a key from the DID document's assertionMethod, and verifiers MUST ignore links without one. Otherwise whoever controls the origin could replace linked metadata, such as an OAuth client metadata document containing client keys, without holding any key authorized by the DID ().

section.name: Retrieval and Validation
section.t: To obtain the AID for an agent URI, a verifier:

li.t: Parses and canonicalizes the agent URI (), rejecting it on failure.
Constructs the AID URL (), applying delegation if the verifier supports it ().
Applies the fetch policy of .
Sends an HTTPS GET with Accept: application/agent-id+json, validating the server certificate for the host of the AID URL.

Treats any status code other than 200 (OK) , and other than 304 (Not Modified) received in response to a conditional request revalidating a cached copy , as a retrieval failure. Redirects are always failures.

Rejects responses larger than 64 KiB, or that are not valid JSON objects. Verifiers MUST NOT reject a response solely because its media type is application/json (to support static hosting) but MUST reject any other media type.
Rejects the document unless its id member is identical to the canonical agent URI.
Performs the anchoring checks of , including the DID binding and pinning checks of when applicable.

section.t: Verifiers SHOULD cache AIDs according to HTTP caching . Operators SHOULD NOT set a freshness lifetime longer than 24 hours, so that key removal takes effect promptly (). Verifiers SHOULD cache failures for a short period to limit repeated fetches.

section.name: Anchoring
section.t: An Agent Key is anchored when the verifier has established that whoever controls the agent URI published it. This document defines two anchoring modes. An AID uses exactly one.

section.name: Origin-Anchored Agents
section.t: The AID contains keys and no did. The keys are anchored by the HTTPS retrieval of : control of the AID Origin is control of the agent's identity.
Each JWK in keys MUST:

li.t: contain only public key parameters;
have a kid equal to its Key Identifier ();
have an alg member; and
be usable for signatures ("use": "sig", or a key_ops containing "verify").

section.t: Implementations MUST support EdDSA (Ed25519) and ES256. Algorithms MUST be restricted as described in ; in particular, none and symmetric algorithms MUST NOT be accepted.
This mode needs nothing beyond a web server. Its weakness is that identity is exactly as durable as control of the domain ().

section.name: DID-Anchored Agents
section.t: The AID contains a did member and no keys. The agent's keys are the verification methods of the DID document, with the purposes defined in .
The binding between the agent URI and the DID MUST be bidirectional:

li.t: the AID retrieved for the agent URI names the DID in did; and
the DID document lists the canonical agent URI in its alsoKnownAs property .

section.t: Verifiers MUST check both directions and MUST treat the agent as unverified if either is missing.

Pinning. A verifier that has previously verified an agent URI as DID-anchored and recorded its DID MUST NOT attribute a later AID for that agent URI to the same agent unless it names the same DID. An AID that is origin-anchored or names a different DID MUST be treated as a different identity (for example, by rejecting it, or by treating it as a new agent with no history), not as a key rotation. Verifiers that record identities SHOULD record the DID.

Continuity and its limits. For a verifier that has pinned the DID, DID anchoring preserves identity across a rename or domain move: the operator publishes an AID under the new agent URI and adds that URI to alsoKnownAs. For a verifier with no prior state, DID anchoring gives no more assurance than origin anchoring, because whoever controls the agent URI's origin can publish an origin-anchored AID instead ().

DID methods. A DID whose resolution depends on the same host as the agent URI (for example, did:web on that host) adds no independence from the origin. Operators SHOULD NOT use such a DID for DID anchoring, and verifiers MUST NOT treat it as providing assurance beyond origin anchoring. DID methods that support verifiable key-rotation history (for example, hosted independently of the agent URI's host) are RECOMMENDED. Verifiers MUST maintain an allowlist of DID methods they support and MUST reject any other method. Network requests made by DID resolvers are subject to .

section.name: Lifecycle, Rotation, and Revocation
section.t: Removing a key from the AID (or DID document) revokes it: every statement and Workload Identity Token it signed stops verifying once verifiers' cached copies expire. Rotation and revocation are therefore the same operation, and operators rotate as follows:

li.t: Publish the new key alongside the old one.
Re-issue all statements and credentials signed by the old key, including statements carried in AIDs copied by mirrors and registries.
Remove the old key once re-issued statements have propagated.

section.t: This document deliberately defines no list of retired keys. Keeping a single way to stop trusting a key means verifiers never have to distinguish a planned retirement from a compromise.
Statements about metadata that changes SHOULD carry an exp so that copies held by third parties are refreshed regularly.
If status is "suspended" or "retired", verifiers MUST treat all signatures, statements, and credentials from the agent as invalid. A retired agent URI SHOULD NOT be reassigned to a different agent.
Operators that need auditable key history MAY additionally record their AIDs and statements in a transparency service . This document does not require it.

section.name: Agent Statements
section.t: An Agent Statement is a JWS in compact serialization, signed with an Agent Key usable for assertion, that binds the agent to a specific version of a resource such as an Agent Card. It allows protocol metadata to be served from any origin, mirrored, or included in registries without losing its link to the agent.
The JWS Protected Header MUST contain:

li.t: typ: "agent-statement+jwt";
alg: the algorithm of the signing key;
kid: the Key Identifier of the signing key ().

section.t: The payload is a JWT Claims Set with:

dd.t: REQUIRED. The canonical agent URI, without a fragment.
REQUIRED. The URL of the resource the statement is about.

REQUIRED. An object with members alg ("sha-256"), canon ("jcs" or "none"), and value (the base64url-encoded digest). With "jcs", the digest is computed over the resource canonicalized per ; with "none", over the exact bytes of the representation.

section.name: Verification
section.t: To verify a statement carried in a link of an AID, a verifier:

li.t: Checks that typ is "agent-statement+jwt".
Checks that iss is identical to the AID's id, and checks the AID's status ().
Checks that sub is identical to the link's href. A statement whose sub differs MUST be rejected, even if it is otherwise valid.
Selects an anchored key usable for assertion whose Key Identifier equals kid, and verifies the signature.
Checks iat and, if present, exp.
Obtains the resource at sub, either by fetching it under the policy of or by using a copy, and compares its digest with resource_digest.

section.t: Statements obtained other than through an AID link (for example, from a registry) are verified in the same way, except that step 2 uses the AID retrieved for iss and step 3 compares sub with the URL the verifier intends to use.

A statement protects only the bytes of the resource it names. It does not extend to other resources that resource refers to, such as a jwks_uri in OAuth client metadata: each such resource needs its own statement, carried in its own link (for example, a jwks link), before it can be relied on with the same assurance.

Protocol metadata documents that support extension fields SHOULD include a reference back to the agent URI, so that a client starting from the metadata can find the identity. How that reference is expressed is defined by each protocol (see ).

section.name: Signing
section.t: An agent proves its identity on an HTTP request by signing it as specified in , with the additional requirements in this section. A request signed this way is a conforming request; this profile adds a new Signature-Agent member type and constrains the signature further.

The request MUST include a Signature-Agent Dictionary member, keyed by the signature label, whose value is the AID URL derived from the agent's canonical agent URI () and which carries the parameter type=agent-id:

figure.name: Signature-Agent member (line break for display only)

section.t: The signature MUST:

li.t: cover @method, @authority, @target-uri, and "signature-agent";key="<label>";
cover content-digest when the request has content;
cover workload-identity-token when that field is present ();
include the created and expires parameters, with expires no more than 300 seconds after created;
include a keyid parameter whose value is the Key Identifier of the signing key; and
include the parameter tag="web-bot-auth".

section.t: A nonce parameter SHOULD be included where the verifier is expected to detect replay.
Example:

figure.name: A signed request (line breaks for display only)
figure.sourcecode: POST /v1/bookings HTTP/1.1 Host: api.example.net Content-Type: application/json Content-Digest: sha-256=:...: Signature-Agent: sig1="https://example.com/.well-known/agent/planner" ;type=agent-id Signature-Input: sig1=("@method" "@authority" "@target-uri" "signature-agent";key="sig1" "content-digest"); created=1792486800;expires=1792486860; keyid="kPrK_qmxVWaYVA9wwBF6Iuo3vVzz7TxHCTwXBygrS4k"; tag="web-bot-auth" Signature: sig1=:...:

section.name: Verification
section.t: A verifier MUST perform all of the following steps, and MUST NOT rely on a generic HTTP Message Signatures implementation to enforce them:

li.t: Select the signature with tag="web-bot-auth" whose label has a Signature-Agent member with type=agent-id. If there is none, the request does not carry an agent identity under this profile.
Determine the agent URI from the member value, without normalizing the value first:
If the value is a well-known AID URL (), derive the agent URI by reverse mapping. A verifier that supports delegation MUST also confirm that delegation does not apply to that host ().

Otherwise, a verifier that supports delegation retrieves the document at the value as in steps 3 to 6 of , takes its id as the agent URI, and MUST confirm that dereferencing that agent URI, including the delegation lookup, yields an AID URL identical to the value.
Any other value is rejected.

Check that the covered components include every component required by , and that expires is no more than 300 seconds after created and the current time is between them, allowing for modest clock skew.
Retrieve the AID () and check status ().

If a Workload-Identity-Token field is present, validate it as described in ; the verification key is then the key in its cnf claim, and keyid MUST equal that key's Key Identifier. Otherwise, select an anchored key usable for authentication whose Key Identifier equals keyid. Key lookup is keyed on the pair (agent URI, keyid), as required by .
Verify the signature as specified in .

If the request has content, recompute the digest of the received content for a supported algorithm as specified in and compare it with the covered Content-Digest value. A request with content and a missing, unsupported, or mismatched Content-Digest MUST be rejected. A valid signature over Content-Digest does not by itself authenticate the content ().

section.t: On success, the verifier has established that the request, including its content, was made by a holder of a key anchored to the agent URI (directly, or through an instance credential). On failure, the verifier MUST NOT treat the request as coming from the named agent; it MAY process it as an unauthenticated request.
A verifier that does not support type=agent-id ignores the member, as that specification requires, and so treats the request as not signed by a known agent rather than failing.

section.name: Profile: Agent Instances
section.t: Agents frequently run as many short-lived instances, for example one per task. Publishing a key for each instance in the AID does not scale, and placing the agent's long-term private keys in every instance is unsafe.
Instead, the agent's controlling infrastructure issues each instance a token in the WIMSE Workload Identity Token (WIT) format that binds the instance's key to the agent.

This profile reuses the WIT format and header field but not the WIMSE trust model. requires verifiers to bind each trust domain to issuers and trust anchors provisioned out of band. This profile replaces that requirement: the only authorized issuers of a WIT whose sub is an agent URI are the assertion keys anchored to exactly that agent URI (), discovered from its AID. Verifiers that also implement WIMSE MUST NOT treat these keys as trust anchors for any other workload identifier, in the same trust domain or otherwise, and MUST NOT accept such a WIT under WIMSE trust-domain configuration alone.
The WIT MUST conform to the format and claim requirements of and additionally:

li.t: is signed with an Agent Key usable for assertion, with the JWS kid header set to that key's Key Identifier;
has a cnf claim containing the instance's public key as a jwk, as required by ;
has sub set to the canonical agent URI;
has iss, if present, set to the canonical agent URI;
has a jti claim, which MUST be generated at random and not reused ();
has an iat claim that is not in the future; and
has an exp later than iat and no more than one hour after it.

section.t: The instance signs requests with its own key as in , with keyid set to the Key Identifier of the key in the WIT's cnf.jwk, and sends the WIT in the Workload-Identity-Token field defined by , which the signature covers.
To validate the WIT, the verifier:

li.t: Validates the WIT's format and claims as specified in and the additional requirements above. The verifier MUST reject the WIT if iat is missing; if iat is later than the current time plus the allowed clock skew; unless 0 < exp - iat <= 3600; if exp has passed; or if nbf is present and has not yet been reached. These checks MUST be performed explicitly, because does not require JWT libraries to reject a future iat.
Checks that sub is identical to the agent URI derived from Signature-Agent, and retrieves its AID; trust-anchor provisioning is replaced as described above.
Selects an anchored key usable for assertion whose Key Identifier equals the WIT's kid, and verifies the WIT signature.
Checks that the request signature's keyid equals the Key Identifier of cnf.jwk, and verifies the request signature with that key using the algorithm in cnf.jwk.alg.

section.t: This profile does not use the WIMSE HTTP signature profile , whose tag and covered components differ; see .

section.name: Profile: Authorization
section.t: Identity is not authorization. This section connects agent identity to OAuth 2.0 without defining new token formats.

section.name: The Agent as an OAuth Client
section.t: An agent that obtains OAuth tokens SHOULD use a Client ID Metadata Document as its client identifier and link to it from its AID with rel="oauth-client-metadata". The client metadata document SHOULD include the agent_uri client metadata parameter () containing the canonical agent URI.

The agent_uri value is a claim made by whoever publishes the client metadata document. Ordinary client authentication does not authenticate it: anyone can publish client metadata that names someone else's agent URI and then authenticate correctly as that client.

Association check. The association between a client_id and an agent is verified by retrieving the AID for the claimed agent URI (), including all anchoring and status checks, and confirming that the AID has an oauth-client-metadata link whose href is identical to the client_id, with any statement that link requires (). An authorization server that does not attribute agent identity MAY skip this check. On its own, the check does not show that the party making the current request controls the agent, because a public client_id can be used by anyone.
Agent attribution. An authorization server MUST NOT treat the current caller as an authenticated agent unless one of the following holds:

li.t: the association check succeeds for the exact client_id, and the client authenticates with private_key_jwt in the current exchange using qualifying client keys (below); or
a request signature for the agent URI is verified under in the current exchange.

section.t: A valid client assertion without a successful association check leaves the agent identity unverified.

Qualifying client keys. A statement protects only the bytes it names (), so a statement over the client metadata document protects a jwks_uri value but not the keys served there. For the private_key_jwt route, client keys qualify only if they are:

li.t: served from a jwks_uri whose origin, compared as in , equals the AID Origin (origin-anchored agents only); or

served from a jwks_uri for which the AID has a link with rel="jwks" whose href is identical to the jwks_uri, and which is trusted under : same-origin or carrying a valid statement for origin-anchored agents, and carrying a valid statement for DID-anchored agents.

section.t: For DID-anchored agents, keys therefore qualify only through a statement-covered client metadata document with embedded jwks, or through a statement-covered jwks link; no other jwks_uri qualifies, even on the AID Origin. Because a statement covers the exact bytes of the JWK Set, any change to the set, including key rotation, requires a new statement (). Agents whose client keys do not qualify MUST use request signatures for agent attribution.

Which agent is attributed. The attributed agent is the one whose identity was verified: for the private_key_jwt route, the agent URI that passed the association check; for the request-signature route, the agent URI derived from Signature-Agent. If the client metadata document's agent_uri is absent or names a different agent, the authorization server MUST NOT display or record that value as the agent's identity, and MAY reject the request.

Consent. In flows where the user's browser reaches the authorization endpoint through a front-channel redirect, the agent cannot sign that request, and the token request happens only after consent. A consent screen can therefore show a verified agent identity only if attribution succeeded on a back-channel request made for the same authorization request before consent. Agents that want verified identity shown at consent SHOULD use Pushed Authorization Requests , with the pushed request either signed under or authenticated with private_key_jwt satisfying the attribution rule above. Authorization servers SHOULD support this.

Otherwise, the authorization server MUST handle the client as it would any client using that client_id, and MUST NOT present it to users as a verified agent identity. When a verified identity is shown, consent screens SHOULD display the attributed agent URI or its DID and MUST present the operator name as claimed by the agent ().

section.name: Delegation
section.t: When an agent acts on behalf of a user or another agent, the delegation SHOULD be expressed with OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange , with the agent identified in the act claim by "sub" set to its canonical agent URI. As required by , only the current actor is relevant to access-control decisions; nested actors are informational.

Access tokens used by agents SHOULD be sender-constrained, for example with DPoP . The DPoP key SHOULD be an instance key () or a key dedicated to DPoP. Agent Keys used for assertion MUST NOT be used as DPoP keys, both to keep long-term keys out of running agents () and to avoid using one key across JWS statements, HTTP message signatures, and DPoP proofs. Within a single trust domain, can carry the agent identity and call context between services.

section.name: Protected Resources
section.t: Resource servers advertise their requirements using OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata . A resource server MAY require a valid agent signature () in addition to an access token, and MAY apply policy based on the agent URI or its DID.

section.name: Discovery
section.t: Dereferencing a known agent URI requires no discovery. To let others find which agents a domain operates, a domain MAY list them in an API catalog (a linkset ) at /.well-known/api-catalog, using the agent URI as the link context and agent-identity links to the AIDs:

figure.name: Listing agents in an API catalog

section.t: Publishing a catalog is optional (). Registries and search services that index agents SHOULD verify AIDs and statements themselves rather than asking clients to trust the index.

dd.t: An Agent Card describes how to communicate with an agent. The AID links to it with rel="agent-card". A2A clients can verify a card by checking the agent's statement about it.
MCP server metadata describes tools and how to reach them. The AID links to it with rel="mcp-server-card". MCP clients can identify the calling agent to MCP servers using request signatures.
The AID links to API descriptions with rel="service-desc" .

lets automated clients sign requests and resolve keys from an HTTPS URL. is a profile of it that adds a Signature-Agent type resolving to an AID, which gives the signer a stable agent name, purpose-scoped keys, and an optional DID anchor.

defines workload credentials. reuses the WIMSE Workload Identity Token format, with the agent URI as the workload identifier and the AID, rather than out-of-band trust anchors, as the source of the issuer's keys.

section.name: Trust Model
section.t: For origin-anchored agents, the trust anchors are DNS and the Web PKI: anyone who can obtain a certificate for the agent URI's host and serve content there can impersonate the agent. This is the same trust model as the web itself and is appropriate for most agents.

DID anchoring reduces this dependency only for verifiers that have pinned the agent's DID (). On first contact, a verifier cannot tell a legitimate origin-anchored agent from an attacker who has taken over the domain and replaced a DID-anchored AID with an origin-anchored one. Even for a pinned DID, assurance holds only if verifiers rely solely on DID-authorized keys and on metadata covered by statements made with them ().

section.name: DNS Delegation
section.t: For a delegated agent (), trust rests on the DNSSEC chain for the agent URI's host and on the Web PKI and hosting of the delegated location. Requiring a secure DNSSEC response prevents an attacker who can spoof or intercept DNS from pointing verifiers at documents it controls. Without that requirement, delegation would be weaker than the well-known mapping, which TLS protects.

An attacker who can block or tamper with DNS can make delegated agents unverifiable, but cannot cause a different AID to be accepted: an insecure response leads only to the well-known mapping, where operators that delegate publish nothing.

TLS authenticates the delegated host, not the path. Whoever can publish under the base path controls the identities of all agents of the delegating host, so operators SHOULD choose a delegated location they control, or one that isolates tenants from each other.

Verifiers that do not support delegation use the well-known mapping. If an attacker who cannot change DNS can still publish under /.well-known/agent on a delegating host, such verifiers would accept the attacker's documents. Operators that delegate SHOULD therefore ensure that nothing can be published at that path on the delegating host.

section.name: Handle Reassignment
section.t: If a domain lapses and is registered by someone else, the new holder can publish an AID for the same agent URIs. Verifiers that record identities for audit or reputation SHOULD record the Key Identifiers (and DID, when present) alongside the agent URI, and SHOULD treat a change of all keys for an agent as a significant event.

section.name: Operator Claims
section.t: Verification establishes possession of a key anchored to an agent URI or DID. It does not establish who operates the agent: operator.name and operator.url are supplied by the same party that publishes the AID. The owner of attacker.example can claim "Example Travel Ltd" as operator and point operator.url at the real company's website.

User interfaces and logs MUST NOT present an operator name as verified unless it has been confirmed by a separate mechanism trusted by the verifier, which this document does not define. They SHOULD display the authenticated agent URI host (in A-label form) or DID alongside any operator name.

section.name: Verifier-Initiated Fetches
section.t: Verification causes network requests to destinations chosen by untrusted parties: AID URLs from Signature-Agent values or delegation records, statement subjects and link targets, and requests made by DID resolvers. Each of these can be used for server-side request forgery or denial of service. The following policy applies to every fetch made in the course of verification:

li.t: Only HTTPS URLs are fetched, with certificate validation.

Destinations whose host is, or resolves to, an address that the IANA IPv4 or IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registries mark as not globally reachable MUST NOT be fetched. Hosts that are special-use names that do not resolve in the global DNS (for example, localhost or names under local or internal) MUST NOT be fetched. Administrators MAY configure explicit exceptions for private deployments.
The resolved address MUST be checked and then used for the connection (pinned), so that DNS changes cannot redirect the request after the check.
HTTP redirects MUST NOT be followed, as in . Any status other than 200, and other than 304 received in response to a conditional revalidation request, is a failure.
Verifiers MUST enforce connection and response timeouts, and MUST bound response sizes: 64 KiB for AIDs and a locally configured limit for other resources.

Verifiers MUST bound the number of fetches per verification. A limit of 4 (for example, the AID, a DID resolution, and a statement subject) is RECOMMENDED. A delegation lookup () and a DID resolution each count as one fetch toward this limit; verifiers MUST separately bound the requests a DID resolver makes, by configuration for each allowed DID method. Verifiers MUST NOT recursively follow links or depends-style references from fetched documents.
Verifiers MUST rate-limit fetches per host and cache results, including failures.

section.t: A statement whose signature is valid does not make its sub safe to fetch: an attacker can publish a legitimate AID under its own domain and sign a statement whose sub names an internal address.

section.name: Request Content and Replay
section.t: HTTP message signatures authenticate header values, not content. Verifiers MUST recompute Content-Digest over received content (); otherwise an attacker can change the content of a signed request while keeping the signed digest.

Signatures cover the method, target URI, and authority, which prevents replay against a different resource or service. The short created-expires window limits replay against the same resource; verifiers for non-idempotent operations SHOULD require and track nonce values.

section.name: Key Compromise and Key Separation
section.t: Compromise of an Agent Key lets the attacker act as the agent until the key is removed and caches expire. Operators SHOULD keep Agent Keys in hardware or a key management service and use instance credentials () so that long-term keys are never present in running agents. Workload Identity Tokens SHOULD be short-lived, because they cannot be individually revoked.

Operators SHOULD use different keys for assertion and authentication, using agent_use for origin-anchored keys and DID verification relationships for DID-anchored keys (), and MUST NOT use Agent Keys as DPoP keys ().

section.name: Cross-Origin Metadata
section.t: Requiring statements bound to the exact href for cross-origin links (, ) prevents a compromised or malicious third-party host, mirror, or registry from attaching metadata to an agent's identity or redirecting a valid statement to other content. A statement only proves that the agent published the resource; it does not vouch for the truth of the resource's contents.

section.name: Confusable Names
section.t: Agent URIs can be visually similar (e.g., agent://examp1e.example/planner and agent://example.example/planner). User interfaces that display agent identities SHOULD display the A-label form of the host, and SHOULD warn when an agent URI or DID is new to the user.

section.name: Privacy Considerations
section.t: The considerations of apply.

li.t: Linkability is the point, for agents. Request signatures make an agent's traffic attributable and linkable across services. That is intended for the agent; it must not extend to the people it acts for. Agent URIs, WIT jti values, and Signature-Agent values MUST NOT encode user identifiers. WIT jti values MUST be random and not reused across users.

Per-user agents. Deployments that create one agent per end user (e.g., agent://example.com/u/alice) make that user's activity linkable across all services the agent visits. Such deployments SHOULD use a shared agent identity and convey user context only through authorization tokens sent to parties entitled to it.

Enumeration. API catalogs () let anyone list a domain's agents. Domains that do not want their agents to be enumerable should not publish them in a catalog; AIDs remain retrievable by those who already know the agent URI.

Verifier fetches. Fetching an AID reveals to the operator that a verifier has seen the agent, and delegation lookups reveal the same to DNS resolvers and to the operator of the delegated location. Caching reduces this signal.

abstract.t: This RFC is the revised specification of the protocol and format used in the implementation of the Domain Name System. It obsoletes RFC-883. This memo documents the details of the domain name client - server communication.

front.title: Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps

abstract.t: This document defines a date and time format for use in Internet protocols that is a profile of the ISO 8601 standard for representation of dates and times using the Gregorian calendar.

A Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) is a compact sequence of characters that identifies an abstract or physical resource. This specification defines the generic URI syntax and a process for resolving URI references that might be in relative form, along with guidelines and security considerations for the use of URIs on the Internet. The URI syntax defines a grammar that is a superset of all valid URIs, allowing an implementation to parse the common components of a URI reference without knowing the scheme-specific requirements of every possible identifier. This specification does not define a generative grammar for URIs; that task is performed by the individual specifications of each URI scheme. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

The Domain Name System Security Extensions (DNSSEC) add data origin authentication and data integrity to the Domain Name System. This document introduces these extensions and describes their capabilities and limitations. This document also discusses the services that the DNS security extensions do and do not provide. Last, this document describes the interrelationships between the documents that collectively describe DNSSEC. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Resource Records for the DNS Security Extensions

abstract.t: This document is part of a family of documents that describe the DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC). The DNS Security Extensions are a collection of resource records and protocol modifications that provide source authentication for the DNS. This document defines the public key (DNSKEY), delegation signer (DS), resource record digital signature (RRSIG), and authenticated denial of existence (NSEC) resource records. The purpose and format of each resource record is described in detail, and an example of each resource record is given.
This document obsoletes RFC 2535 and incorporates changes from all updates to RFC 2535. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Protocol Modifications for the DNS Security Extensions

abstract.t: This document is part of a family of documents that describe the DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC). The DNS Security Extensions are a collection of new resource records and protocol modifications that add data origin authentication and data integrity to the DNS. This document describes the DNSSEC protocol modifications. This document defines the concept of a signed zone, along with the requirements for serving and resolving by using DNSSEC. These techniques allow a security-aware resolver to authenticate both DNS resource records and authoritative DNS error indications.
This document obsoletes RFC 2535 and incorporates changes from all updates to RFC 2535. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Augmented BNF for Syntax Specifications: ABNF

abstract.t: Internet technical specifications often need to define a formal syntax. Over the years, a modified version of Backus-Naur Form (BNF), called Augmented BNF (ABNF), has been popular among many Internet specifications. The current specification documents ABNF. It balances compactness and simplicity with reasonable representational power. The differences between standard BNF and ABNF involve naming rules, repetition, alternatives, order-independence, and value ranges. This specification also supplies additional rule definitions and encoding for a core lexical analyzer of the type common to several Internet specifications. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Internationalized Domain Names for Applications (IDNA): Definitions and Document Framework

abstract.t: This document is one of a collection that, together, describe the protocol and usage context for a revision of Internationalized Domain Names for Applications (IDNA), superseding the earlier version. It describes the document collection and provides definitions and other material that are common to the set. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA): Protocol

abstract.t: This document is the revised protocol definition for Internationalized Domain Names (IDNs). The rationale for changes, the relationship to the older specification, and important terminology are provided in other documents. This document specifies the protocol mechanism, called Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA), for registering and looking up IDNs in a way that does not require changes to the DNS itself. IDNA is only meant for processing domain names, not free text. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Media Type Specifications and Registration Procedures

abstract.t: This document defines procedures for the specification and registration of media types for use in HTTP, MIME, and other Internet protocols. This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice.

This memo reiterates the assignment of an IPv4 address block (192.0.0.0/24) to IANA. It also instructs IANA to restructure its IPv4 and IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registries. Upon restructuring, the aforementioned registries will record all special-purpose address blocks, maintaining a common set of information regarding each address block.

JSON Web Signature (JWS) represents content secured with digital signatures or Message Authentication Codes (MACs) using JSON-based data structures. Cryptographic algorithms and identifiers for use with this specification are described in the separate JSON Web Algorithms (JWA) specification and an IANA registry defined by that specification. Related encryption capabilities are described in the separate JSON Web Encryption (JWE) specification.

A JSON Web Key (JWK) is a JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) data structure that represents a cryptographic key. This specification also defines a JWK Set JSON data structure that represents a set of JWKs. Cryptographic algorithms and identifiers for use with this specification are described in the separate JSON Web Algorithms (JWA) specification and IANA registries established by that specification.

JSON Web Token (JWT) is a compact, URL-safe means of representing claims to be transferred between two parties. The claims in a JWT are encoded as a JSON object that is used as the payload of a JSON Web Signature (JWS) structure or as the plaintext of a JSON Web Encryption (JWE) structure, enabling the claims to be digitally signed or integrity protected with a Message Authentication Code (MAC) and/or encrypted.

This specification defines mechanisms for dynamically registering OAuth 2.0 clients with authorization servers. Registration requests send a set of desired client metadata values to the authorization server. The resulting registration responses return a client identifier to use at the authorization server and the client metadata values registered for the client. The client can then use this registration information to communicate with the authorization server using the OAuth 2.0 protocol. This specification also defines a set of common client metadata fields and values for clients to use during registration.

front.title: Guidelines and Registration Procedures for URI Schemes

abstract.t: This document updates the guidelines and recommendations, as well as the IANA registration processes, for the definition of Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes. It obsoletes RFC 4395.

This specification defines a method for computing a hash value over a JSON Web Key (JWK). It defines which fields in a JWK are used in the hash computation, the method of creating a canonical form for those fields, and how to convert the resulting Unicode string into a byte sequence to be hashed. The resulting hash value can be used for identifying or selecting the key represented by the JWK that is the subject of the thumbprint.

front.title: Proof-of-Possession Key Semantics for JSON Web Tokens (JWTs)

abstract.t: This specification describes how to declare in a JSON Web Token (JWT) that the presenter of the JWT possesses a particular proof-of- possession key and how the recipient can cryptographically confirm proof of possession of the key by the presenter. Being able to prove possession of a key is also sometimes described as the presenter being a holder-of-key.

front.title: CFRG Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) and Signatures in JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE)

abstract.t: This document defines how to use the Diffie-Hellman algorithms "X25519" and "X448" as well as the signature algorithms "Ed25519" and "Ed448" from the IRTF CFRG elliptic curves work in JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE).

front.title: The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format

abstract.t: JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a lightweight, text-based, language-independent data interchange format. It was derived from the ECMAScript Programming Language Standard. JSON defines a small set of formatting rules for the portable representation of structured data.
This document removes inconsistencies with other specifications of JSON, repairs specification errors, and offers experience-based interoperability guidance.
This specification defines a model for the relationships between resources on the Web ("links") and the type of those relationships ("link relation types").
It also defines the serialisation of such links in HTTP headers with the Link header field.

front.title: Scoped Interpretation of DNS Resource Records through "Underscored" Naming of Attribute Leaves

abstract.t: Formally, any DNS Resource Record (RR) may occur under any domain name. However, some services use an operational convention for defining specific interpretations of an RRset by locating the records in a DNS branch under the parent domain to which the RRset actually applies. The top of this subordinate branch is defined by a naming convention that uses a reserved node name, which begins with the underscore character (e.g., "_name"). The underscored naming construct defines a semantic scope for DNS record types that are associated with the parent domain above the underscored branch. This specification explores the nature of this DNS usage and defines the "Underscored and Globally Scoped DNS Node Names" registry with IANA. The purpose of this registry is to avoid collisions resulting from the use of the same underscored name for different services.
This memo defines a path prefix for "well-known locations", "/.well-known/", in selected Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes.
In doing so, it obsoletes RFC 5785 and updates the URI schemes defined in RFC 7230 to reserve that space. It also updates RFC 7595 to track URI schemes that support well-known URIs in their registry.

This specification defines a protocol for an HTTP- and JSON-based Security Token Service (STS) by defining how to request and obtain security tokens from OAuth 2.0 authorization servers, including security tokens employing impersonation and delegation.

front.title: JSON Web Token Best Current Practices

abstract.t: JSON Web Tokens, also known as JWTs, are URL-safe JSON-based security tokens that contain a set of claims that can be signed and/or encrypted. JWTs are being widely used and deployed as a simple security token format in numerous protocols and applications, both in the area of digital identity and in other application areas. This Best Current Practices document updates RFC 7519 to provide actionable guidance leading to secure implementation and deployment of JWTs.

Cryptographic operations like hashing and signing need the data to be expressed in an invariant format so that the operations are reliably repeatable. One way to address this is to create a canonical representation of the data. Canonicalization also permits data to be exchanged in its original form on the "wire" while cryptographic operations performed on the canonicalized counterpart of the data in the producer and consumer endpoints generate consistent results.

This document describes the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS). This specification defines how to create a canonical representation of JSON data by building on the strict serialization methods for JSON primitives defined by ECMAScript, constraining JSON data to the Internet JSON (I-JSON) subset, and by using deterministic property sorting.

The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is a stateless application-level protocol for distributed, collaborative, hypertext information systems. This document describes the overall architecture of HTTP, establishes common terminology, and defines aspects of the protocol that are shared by all versions. In this definition are core protocol elements, extensibility mechanisms, and the "http" and "https" Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes.
This document updates RFC 3864 and obsoletes RFCs 2818, 7231, 7232, 7233, 7235, 7538, 7615, 7694, and portions of 7230.

The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is a stateless application-level protocol for distributed, collaborative, hypertext information systems. This document defines HTTP caches and the associated header fields that control cache behavior or indicate cacheable response messages.
This document obsoletes RFC 7234.

This document describes a mechanism for creating, encoding, and verifying digital signatures or message authentication codes over components of an HTTP message. This mechanism supports use cases where the full HTTP message may not be known to the signer and where the message may be transformed (e.g., by intermediaries) before reaching the verifier. This document also describes a means for requesting that a signature be applied to a subsequent HTTP message in an ongoing HTTP exchange.

This document defines HTTP fields that support integrity digests. The Content-Digest field can be used for the integrity of HTTP message content. The Repr-Digest field can be used for the integrity of HTTP representations. Want-Content-Digest and Want-Repr-Digest can be used to indicate a sender's interest and preferences for receiving the respective Integrity fields.
This document obsoletes RFC 3230 and the Digest and Want-Digest HTTP fields.

This document describes a set of data types and associated algorithms that are intended to make it easier and safer to define and handle HTTP header and trailer fields, known as "Structured Fields", "Structured Headers", or "Structured Trailers". It is intended for use by specifications of new HTTP fields.
This document obsoletes RFC 8941.

front.title: HTTP Message Signatures for automated traffic

abstract.t:
This document describes a protocol for identifying automated traffic using [HTTP-MESSAGE-SIGNATURES]. The goal is to allow automated HTTP clients to cryptographically sign outbound requests, allowing HTTP servers to verify their identity with confidence.
It defines the Signature-Agent header field for in-band key discovery, a key directory format based on JWKS, and a well-known URI at which that directory is served.

The WIMSE architecture defines authentication and authorization for software workloads in a variety of runtime environments, from the most basic ones up to complex multi-service, multi-cloud, multi- tenant deployments.
This document defines the credentials that workloads use to represent their identity. They can be used in various protocols to authenticate workloads to each other. To use these credentials, workloads must provide proof of possession of the associated private key material, which is covered in other documents. This document focuses on the credentials alone, independent of the proof-of- possession mechanism.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.

front.title: Additional Media Type Structured Syntax Suffixes

abstract.t: A content media type name sometimes includes partitioned meta- information distinguished by a structured syntax to permit noting an attribute of the media as a suffix to the name. This document defines several structured syntax suffixes for use with media type registrations. In particular, it defines and registers the "+json", "+ber", "+der", "+fastinfoset", "+wbxml" and "+zip" structured syntax suffixes, and provides a media type structured syntax suffix registration form for the "+xml" structured syntax suffix. This document is not an Internet Standards Track specification; it is published for informational purposes.

front.title: Specification for DNS over Transport Layer Security (TLS)

abstract.t: This document describes the use of Transport Layer Security (TLS) to provide privacy for DNS. Encryption provided by TLS eliminates opportunities for eavesdropping and on-path tampering with DNS queries in the network, such as discussed in RFC 7626. In addition, this document specifies two usage profiles for DNS over TLS and provides advice on performance considerations to minimize overhead from using TCP and TLS with DNS.

This document focuses on securing stub-to-recursive traffic, as per the charter of the DPRIVE Working Group. It does not prevent future applications of the protocol to recursive-to-authoritative traffic.

This document offers guidance for developing privacy considerations for inclusion in protocol specifications. It aims to make designers, implementers, and users of Internet protocols aware of privacy-related design choices. It suggests that whether any individual RFC warrants a specific privacy considerations section will depend on the document's content.

This specification defines the Security Event Token (SET) data structure. A SET describes statements of fact from the perspective of an issuer about a subject. These statements of fact represent an event that occurred directly to or about a security subject, for example, a statement about the issuance or revocation of a token on behalf of a subject. This specification is intended to enable representing security- and identity-related events. A SET is a JSON Web Token (JWT), which can be optionally signed and/or encrypted. SETs can be distributed via protocols such as HTTP.

front.title: Linkset: Media Types and a Link Relation Type for Link Sets

abstract.t: This specification defines two formats and associated media types for representing sets of links as standalone documents. One format is based on JSON, and the other is aligned with the format for representing links in the HTTP "Link" header field. This specification also introduces a link relation type to support the discovery of sets of links.

This document describes a mechanism for sender-constraining OAuth 2.0 tokens via a proof-of-possession mechanism on the application level. This mechanism allows for the detection of replay attacks with access and refresh tokens.

front.title: api-catalog: A Well-Known URI and Link Relation to Help Discovery of APIs

abstract.t: This document defines the "api-catalog" well-known URI and link relation. It is intended to facilitate automated discovery and usage of published Application Programming Interfaces (APIs). A request to the api-catalog resource will return a document providing information about, and links to, the Publisher's APIs.
This specification defines a metadata format that an OAuth 2.0 client or authorization server can use to obtain the information needed to interact with an OAuth 2.0 protected resource.

This document defines the pushed authorization request (PAR) endpoint, which allows clients to push the payload of an OAuth 2.0 authorization request to the authorization server via a direct request and provides them with a request URI that is used as reference to the data in a subsequent call to the authorization endpoint.

front.title: An Architecture for Trustworthy and Transparent Digital Supply Chains

abstract.t: Traceability in supply chains is a growing security concern. While Verifiable Data Structures (VDSs) have addressed specific issues, such as equivocation over digital certificates, they lack a universal architecture for all supply chains. This document defines such an architecture for single-issuer signed statement transparency. It ensures extensibility and interoperability between different transparency services as well as compliance with various auditing procedures and regulatory requirements.

This specification defines a mechanism through which an OAuth client can identify itself to authorization servers, without prior dynamic client registration or other existing registration. This is through the usage of a URL as a client_id in an OAuth flow, where the URL refers to a document containing the necessary client metadata, enabling the authorization server to fetch the metadata about the client as needed.

front.title: WIMSE Workload-to-Workload Authentication with HTTP Signatures

abstract.t: The WIMSE architecture defines authentication and authorization for software workloads in a variety of runtime environments, from the most basic ones to complex multi-service, multi-cloud, multi-tenant deployments. This document defines one of the mechanisms to provide workload authentication, using HTTP Signatures. While only applicable to HTTP traffic, the protocol provides end-to-end protection of requests (and optionally, responses), even when service traffic is not end-to-end encrypted, that is, when TLS proxies and load balancers are used. Authentication is based on the Workload Identity Token (WIT).

Transaction Tokens (Txn-Tokens) are designed to maintain and propagate user identity, workload identity and authorization context throughout the Call Chain within a trusted domain during the processing of external requests (e.g. such as API calls) or requests initiated internally within the Trust Domain. Txn-Tokens ensure that this context is preserved throughout the Call Chain thereby enhancing security and consistency in complex, multi-service architectures.

section.name: Open Issues
section.t: This appendix will be removed before publication.

li.t: Signature-Agent type registry. has no registry for type values. Work with the webbotauth WG to create one, or to define agent-id there. Until then, verifiers that only implement ignore agent identities.

WIMSE alignment. Discuss with the WIMSE WG whether agent URIs are acceptable workload identifiers (their authority fits the trust domain shape of WIMSE identifiers), whether AID-based issuer discovery can become a recognized alternative to out-of-band trust-anchor provisioning, and whether instances should also be able to use the WIMSE HTTP signature profile .

Back-references from protocol metadata. Agree with the A2A and MCP projects on how an Agent Card or MCP server card names its agent URI, and who registers the agent-card and mcp-server-card link relations.

Cryptographic test vectors. covers URI processing and delegation records. Once an implementation can produce and cross-check them, add vectors for: statement iss/sub binding; DID key conversion and per-purpose selection; agent_use enforcement, including duplicate key material and malformed values; a preserved DID with substituted same-origin client metadata keys; a DID-anchored client using jwks_uri with private_key_jwt, with and without a statement-covered jwks link; an origin-anchored client whose statement-covered metadata points to a jwks_uri off the AID Origin (not attributed); an attacker-owned client metadata document claiming an unrelated origin-anchored agent's agent_uri, both with only a client assertion (not attributed) and with a request signed by the attacker's own agent (attributed to the attacker's agent, never the claimed one); a WIT with a future iat; an insecure delegation record (ignored); a delegated Signature-Agent value whose forward mapping differs (rejected); content tampering with a valid signature; fetches to forbidden destinations; and expired credentials. Two independent verifiers should reach the same decision for each.
Removed ports from agent URIs, so that an agent's identity depends only on its host and name. The agent-instance profile no longer needs a port restriction.
Added DNS delegation of AID URLs through DNSSEC-validated _agent TXT records (), with matching request-signing, security, privacy, and IANA text.
Added the jwks link relation, so that OAuth client keys behind a jwks_uri can be protected by a statement, including for DID-anchored agents.
Completed the IANA registration templates.

Closed open issues: retired keys (the re-issue model is kept, giving a single way to stop trusting a key), the reserved root segment and name-path rules (kept as specified), DNS-based verification (now specified), and ports (removed).
Updated the test vectors for port removal and added delegation-record vectors.

section.name: Changes from draft-narvaneni-agent-uri-03
section.t: This revision changes the scope of the document from "addressing and discovery" to "identity".
Removed:

li.t: agent+<protocol> transport-binding schemes and the Transport Bindings registry.
Invocation semantics (GET/POST rules, fallback behaviour), query parameters in agent URIs, and conformance levels.
The /.well-known/agents.json registry, replaced by the deterministic mapping of and optional RFC 9727 catalogs.
The agent descriptor's capability fields (skills, transport, interactionModel, versioning, content negotiation). Protocol metadata documents are linked instead.
DID authorities in agent URIs, replaced by DID anchoring ().
Cross-cutting conventions (tracing, idempotency, rate limits, health) and the Interaction Models registry.
The monotonic scope narrowing rule, which conflicted with .

section.t: Added:

li.t: Strict URI syntax, normalization, comparison, and reverse-mapping rules.
The Agent Identity Document, a single Key Identifier scheme, key purposes (including agent_use for origin-anchored keys), and origin and DID anchoring with DID pinning.
Agent Statements bound to the links that carry them.
A request-signing profile of , and an agent-instance profile reusing the WIMSE Workload Identity Token format with AID-based trust.
OAuth bindings that separate metadata association from agent attribution, define which client keys qualify, and describe verified identity at consent using Pushed Authorization Requests.
Security and privacy considerations specific to agent identity, including a fetch policy covering every verifier-initiated request.
Test vectors for URI processing ().
